explanation.SyntaxError: Python could not read this line as Python. Look for a missing bracket or quote, or a colon at the end of the line.
explanation.IndentationError: The spacing at the start of these lines does not line up. Give every line in the same block the same number of spaces.
explanation.TabError: This code mixes tabs and spaces for indentation. Pick one of them and use it on every line.
explanation.NameError: Python does not recognise this name. Check the spelling, and make sure it was given a value before it was used.
explanation.TypeError: These values are different types, and Python cannot combine them this way. Check whether a number and a piece of text are being mixed.
explanation.ValueError: The type is right but the value is not. Check what went in — int() raises this when the text is not a number.
explanation.IndexError: This position is past the end of the list or text. The first position is 0, so the last one is one less than the length.
explanation.KeyError: The dictionary has no key by that name. Check how the key is spelled, and which keys were actually stored.
explanation.ZeroDivisionError: Something was divided by zero. Check the value you are dividing by, especially when it is calculated.
explanation.AttributeError: This value does not have the thing asked for after the dot. Check what sits before the dot and how the name after it is spelled.
explanation.ModuleNotFoundError: Python cannot find the module being imported. Check the spelling of the name after import.
explanation.ImportError: The module was found, but not the name being imported from it. Check the name after from … import.
explanation.EOFError: The program asked for input and there was none left. Type a value in the terminal, or add another line to the test input.
explanation.RecursionError: A function kept calling itself and never stopped. Add a condition that returns without calling again.
explanation.unknown: Something went wrong while the code was running. Go through the values and commands on the line the error points at.

coach.example_heading: You can write it like this
coach.goto: Go to this spot in the editor
coach.terminal_pointer: See the Error interpretation tab for what to do next.

missing-colon.title: This line needs a colon (:) at the end
missing-colon.what: Python could not find where the indented block was meant to start.
missing-colon.why: Statements that carry indented code beneath them — if, for, while, def — take a colon after the condition or the name.
missing-colon.where: check for a colon (:) at the end of the line.
missing-colon.next: Add a colon to the end of the highlighted line and run it again.

expected-indented-block.title: The code inside this block needs indenting
expected-indented-block.what: Python reached a block that had no statements in it.
expected-indented-block.why: Whatever belongs to an if, a loop, or a function is written four spaces further in than the line that opened it.
expected-indented-block.where: check whether the line needs spaces in front of it.
expected-indented-block.next: Move the highlighted line four spaces further in than the line above it, and run it again.

unexpected-indent.title: This line is indented further than it should be
unexpected-indent.what: Python found indentation where no new block had been opened.
unexpected-indent.why: A statement that is not inside a block has to start in the same column as the statements around it.
unexpected-indent.where: check whether this line starts further in than its neighbours.
unexpected-indent.next: Line the highlighted row up with the code around it and run it again.

tabs-and-spaces.title: Tabs and spaces are mixed in the indentation
tabs-and-spaces.what: Two kinds of indentation that look alike on screen are being used together.
tabs-and-spaces.why: Python may count a tab and a run of spaces as different widths, so one file has to pick one and stay with it.
tabs-and-spaces.where: delete the indentation on this line and type it again with spaces.
tabs-and-spaces.next: Clear the indentation on the highlighted line, retype it as four spaces, and run it again.

unclosed-delimiter.title: An opening bracket has no closing partner
unclosed-delimiter.what: A parenthesis, square bracket, or brace was opened and never closed.
unclosed-delimiter.why: Every ( [ { needs its matching ) ] }, and Python keeps reading until it finds one.
unclosed-delimiter.where: count the brackets here and on the line above — the opening one may be earlier than the error.
unclosed-delimiter.next: Compare the opening and closing brackets on the highlighted line and the one above it.

unterminated-string.title: This text is missing its closing quote
unterminated-string.what: Python could not find where the piece of text was meant to end.
unterminated-string.why: Text that opens with a single or double quote has to close with the same kind of quote.
unterminated-string.where: check that the quotes on this line come in pairs.
unterminated-string.next: Close the quote on the highlighted line and run it again.

assignment-in-condition.title: Storing a value and comparing values are different
assignment-in-condition.what: Python found the assignment sign in a place that cannot take one.
assignment-in-condition.why: A single = stores a value; == is what asks whether two values are the same.
assignment-in-condition.where: check whether a condition here uses = where it means ==.
assignment-in-condition.next: Decide whether this line stores a value or asks a question, then use the matching sign.

missing-separator.title: Values here need something between them
missing-separator.what: Two values are written next to each other with nothing to separate them.
missing-separator.why: Arguments to a function and items in a list are divided by commas.
missing-separator.where: check whether a comma is missing between two values.
missing-separator.next: Add the missing comma on the highlighted line and run it again.

generic-syntax.title: Python could not read this line
generic-syntax.what: A symbol, quote, bracket, or keyword may be missing or in the wrong place.
generic-syntax.why: Python only runs code that follows its sentence shapes exactly, one line at a time.
generic-syntax.where: read the highlighted line and the one above it together.
generic-syntax.next: Check the colons, brackets, quotes, and indentation in turn, then run it again.
